while saying lewd TikTok video 'not acceptable' and now removed5h agoStreeting visits Kharkiv, 20km from frontline in Ukraine6h agoDeaths linked to heat pass a record 5,000 in England this year, UKHSA says6h agoBurnham meets Prince William at No 107h agoFarage condemns rise of ethnonationalism, as he tells Braverman to shut up about Englishness being for whites7h agoFarage suggests he would not work with Tories in campaign against rejoining EU because he 'will never trust them again'7h agoFarage says people 'disappointed' by Brexit, but 'they're never going to vote to rejoin, believe you me'7h agoFarage claims Tory party 'dominated by those who believed in remain'7h agoTories launch review to draw up plans for 'largest prison building programme in modern history'7h agoVictims' commissioners says she's close to telling people not to report crimes because system not responding properly8h agoMinister condemns lyrics of influencer's song outside No 108h agoBurnham sets target for million more girls in sport by Women's World Cup 20359h agoStephen Timms says Pip review being published today will ‘rehumanise’ benefit Stephen Timms during his statement on the Timms review Photograph: House of Commons/PAView image in fullscreenStephen Timms during his statement on the Timms review Photograph: House of Commons/PAAndrew SparrowTue 24 Nov 2026 17.41 GMTFirst published on Tue 24 Nov 2026 08.59 GMTShareFrom 4h ago14.10 GMTTimms gives statement to MPs on his Pip review, setting out its three key conclusionsIn the Commons, Stephen Timms is now delivering his statement on Pip.

He says Pip provides “vital support to deaf and disabled people and people with long term health conditions”. It was introduced 13 years ago, but has not been reviewed since then.

He says it was co-produced by himself, his two co-chair and 12 other members of a steering group. Almost all of those 12 people had “lived experience of disability or long term ill health”. Every member – including Timms himself – had just one vote, he says.

double quotation mark The review is clear that Pip remains a vital source of support, but it finds that the system is failing in three fundamental respects.

First of all, the assessment is not fit for purpose. It doesn’t consider people’s needs, their aspirations, their barriers, or their extra costs. It’s just about what somebody cannot do. Many people find it adversarial and dehumanising. It struggles to reflect fluctuating and cumulative conditions properly, and it too often leaves people fearing that work, health, treatment or greater independence will count against them. Far from supporting independence, it can be a barrier to it.

Second, awards do not consistently enable the right contribution toward the additional costs that people face. The areas of extra cost survey reviewed by the steering group showed that Pip does not always target the highest levels of support on those with the most severe needs. The future system should make the basis for support clearer, with decisions reflecting individual circumstances better.

And third, the system’s offers offers too little scope for personalised solutions. The review recommends that cash should remain central, but that people should have the choice to access practical services as part of the overall support that they receive. That would allow the system to respond more flexibly to individual needs.

  Stephen Timms, the minister for social security and disability, has published a long-awaited report on Pip (personal independence payment), a disability benefit. His conclusions have been welcomed by disability charities. But the Conservatives have argued that his conclusions are “poles apart” from those in the Alan Milburn report (which said Pip should be scrapped for under-25s), and in the Commons Timms failed to assure Labour MPs who demanded assurances that people currently getting Pip would not lose out.

Nigel Farage has said he might have a “civil chat” with Rupert Lowe but ruled out a deal with Restore Britain while some of its supporters promote antisemitism and think race should be linked to nationality.

There will soon be “no point” in the public reporting crimes to the police, the victims commissioner for England and Wales has said, as she urged ministers to reform the justice system.

For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.

Photograph: House of Commons/PAShare25m ago17.30 GMTSir Jim Mackey is going to stand down as chief executive of NHS England in March next year, it has been been announced. He was appointed last year on secondment.

A spokesperson from the Department of Health and Social Care said:

double quotation markSir Jim has always been clear he was appointed to lead reform of the NHS and set it on the road to recovery during a period of significant challenge.

From the beginning he said this would be a transitional process ahead of a substantive appointment for the new chief executive role in the merged NHS England and DHSC.

The formal recruitment for his successor will begin shortly, but Sir Jim is committed to ensuring a smooth transition and will provide full support to the next CEO.

33m ago17.23 GMTBadenoch claims 'too many people' think criminals not to blame for crime, as Tories declare 'liberal consensus over'Kemi Badenoch may also be feeling aggrieved because (see 4.44pm) because Nigel Farage’s decision to give a press conference at the same time as hers meant that the Tory announcement (see 10.45am) received a lot less attention than it otherwise might have done. But it is worth posting about it because Badenoch and Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary, both gave speeches intended to bury the “liberal, progressive consensus”. Their notion of what this consensus actually is arguably rather eccentric, but their arguments are worth noting.

double quotation markToo many people act as if the real victims of crime are the criminals.

That they are driven to their actions by unfortunate circumstances, poverty, mental health, some say the reason they are assaulting women is that they are sex addicts.

This is an insult to the law-abiding majority, many of whom are poor, many of whom are living with mental health conditions.

Some people believe that instead of punishing criminals and holding them to account we should let them off the hook.

Badenoch did not say who any of these “too many people” actually are, and it sounded as if she was talking about a caricature of extreme leftwing thinking from about 40 years ago. At one point in his speech, Timothy made the same argument. He said:

double quotation markWe’ve succumbed to the progressive idea that it’s not a criminal who’s to blame for their crimes, but society.

At another point in his speech, Timothy was a bit more sympathetic towards liberals – saying some of them weren’t “bad people” – but he claimed they were part of the liberal consensus against which he was declaring war.

double quotation markThe Prison Reform Trust, the Howard League, Nacro, all the main prison reform organisations are set up to demand liberal and progressive change.

And more often than not, ministers are the same. Lord Timpson, Jake Richards, David Lammy, Alex Norris.

They’re not bad people, but if you listen to them their focus is always on who should not be sent to prison.

Not only is it the opposite of what most law-abiding, decent people believe, it’s the precise opposite of what we know works.

Today we declare this liberal, progressive consensus over, and we present a truly conservative alternative.

The thrust of Timothy’s speech was “prison works”. This is a line popularised by Michael Howard when he was home secretary 30 years ago, and Howard has issued a statement this evening endorsing today’s announcement. More controversially, Timothy also said he was sceptical about the idea that prisons can rehabilitate people.

double quotation markI actually agree that prisons should be more effective.

But I want to be clear that I am deeply sceptical about talk of rehabilitation.

It’s a vague word, and there is little evidence that it works as Sir Martin Narey, who used to run the prison service, says.

Outside the venue where Badenoch and Timothy were giving their speeches, protesters held up placards saying ‘Burglars 4 Badenoch” and “Crooks Luv Kemi”. They seemed to be making a point about how prisoner releases started under the Tories, because the last government did not build enough places. They did not say who they were representing, but Nigel Farage’s sidekick Raheem Kassam has been tweeting about them, which may be a clue as to who was behind the stunt.

Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAShare1h ago16.44 GMTBadenoch criticises Farage for jibe about her husband voting remain, saying families should be off limitsKemi Badenoch has criticised Nigel Farage for making a jibe about her remain-voting husband at his press conference this morning. (See 10.51am.) As Sky News reports, asked about Farage’s comment, she told broadcasters:

double quotation markPoliticians go into politics, and our families should not be fair game.

Someone has recently been sentenced to prison because of death threats sent not just to me, but actually to my husband directly. We need to keep people’s families out of this.

And I think that it is a shame that Nigel Farage is feeling so irrelevant and desperate that he is now talking about attacking my husband for voting remain.

View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAShareUpdated at 16.47 GMT2h ago16.25 GMTDisability charities welcome Timms review recommendationsDisability and health charities have broadly welcomed the Timms review. Here are some of their comments.

From Jon Sparkes, chief executive of Mencap, the learning disability charity

double quotation markPeople with a learning disability face significant unavoidable extra costs every day. Many tell us that applying for support through Pip is difficult, while repeated reassessments can feel unnecessary and stressful. Changes to make it kinder and more humane are desperately needed.

We are very pleased that the Timms review has listened to the thousands of people who have campaigned with us for an end to unnecessary reassessments for people with lifelong conditions.

From David Newbold, director of community at Parkinson’s UK
